We begin by defining the Attribution Drift Operator, which measures the L2 norm discrepancy between the expected payout manifold—derived from deterministic clickstream integrals—and the stochastic reality of received payments. This operator forms the foundational kernel of our system, translating vague accounting gaps into precise, quantifiable vectors. To prevent systemic collapse during this measurement, we introduce the Production Isolation Boundary. Mathematically, this acts as a Neumann boundary condition, enforcing a zero-flux constraint on code mutations entering the production phase space. By strictly avoiding live Stripe endpoints and real affiliate links, we ensure the reconciliation logic can be stress-tested against synthetic distributions without risking actual capital. Finally, the Revenue Clarity Metric aggregates these localized conservation checks into a global scalar representing organizational health. It maps the reduction of financial information entropy directly onto operational leverage. The duality here is profound: the ledger is simultaneously a defensive shield against fraud (minimizing drift) and an offensive tool for maximizing founder leverage (maximizing clarity). Failure modes arise primarily at the boundaries—when cross-domain tracking fails, the expected payout integral becomes ill-posed, leading to singularities in the drift operator that require manual, non-computable intervention.
